name: Ants Climbing a Tree Pork Noodles
writer_notes: SELECTOR: One-pan saucy noodle dish, noodles absorb the sauce so it portions clean and reheats without drying. Source publishes 479 cal / 16g protein at a light 4 oz pork per 2 servings; doubling the ground pork gets it over the bar cheaply since ground-pork is a tracked commodity. Glass noodles have no exact board id (tracked rice-noodles is the nearest sub). | HARVEST:
OVERRIDE Ground Pork: [BUMP x1.4] source 160 g for 2 servings is noodle-condiment scale; house 220 g
intro_html: The name is the best part. Little bits of seasoned pork cling to the noodles as you lift them, and somebody in Sichuan decided that looked like ants climbing a tree. What it actually is: a one-pan noodle dinner where the noodles finish cooking right in the broth, so they drink up every drop of the doubanjiang and soy. That is also why it reheats without turning into a dry brick. Traditionally this is made with glass noodles, and rice noodles are the version your regular grocery store actually stocks.
ingredients_display: Doubanjiang (Lee Kum Kee (Chili Bean Sauce Toban Djan)): 4 oz (112 g)
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Chicken Broth, 3.6 cartons: ~$4.51. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 4 32oz cartons.
Pantry seasonings (salt, black pepper): ~$0.23. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $34.27 across 14 servings, so roughly $2.45 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $36.86 across 14 servings, roughly $2.63 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $19.68 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $56.54. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a bowl (at everyday cost) for a Sichuan noodle dinner that a takeout menu would list at four times the price, with half the pork.
shop_smart: Ground pork is the quiet bargain of the meat case. It runs well under ground beef per pound and it carries a spicy sauce better, which is why this bowl lands where it does on cost.
Doubanjiang is a one-jar purchase that outlives the batch. That fermented chili bean paste is the whole flavor of the dish, and a single jar seasons this pot many times over.
Buy the rice noodles in the plain box, not the meal kit. Same noodle, and the kit is mostly a sauce packet you are about to make from scratch anyway.
A knob of fresh ginger keeps for weeks. Store it unpeeled in the freezer and grate off what you need, which beats letting a whole piece go soft in the crisper drawer.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Soak the rice noodles in warm water until pliable but not soft, then drain and set aside.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large pot over medium heat and cook the ginger for about thirty seconds, until it smells sharp.
Stir in the doubanjiang and cook it in the oil for another minute so the paste turns deep red and loses its raw edge.
Add the ground pork, break it up, and cook until no pink remains.
Pour in the chicken broth, soy sauce, and sugar, and bring it up to a simmer.
Add the drained noodles, turn the heat to low, and simmer uncovered until the noodles are tender and most of the liquid has been absorbed.
Kill the heat, fold in the green onions, and season with salt and black pepper to taste.
portion_html: Set the full pot back on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight from Step 1, and divide what is left by 14. Scoop that exact number into each container so nobody gets the sad noodle bowl. Every serving lands near {{cal}} calories with {{protein}} grams of protein. Let them cool with the lids off before you stack them, or the steam turns the noodles to mush.

steps: Soak the rice noodles in warm water until pliable, then drain.
Cook the ginger in hot oil, then fry the doubanjiang until it turns deep red.
Brown the ground pork in the same pot until no pink remains.
Add broth, soy sauce, and sugar and bring to a simmer.
Add the noodles and simmer until tender and most of the liquid is absorbed.
Fold in green onions, season, and portion into 14 containers.
